---
title: "Why October Belongs to Horror"
subtitle: "Some feelings we seek out at certain times. Some we need all year."
---

::: {.reel}
Feature Story
:::

```{r}
source("prep.R")

movies |>
  filter(genre %in% c("Horror", "Comedy")) |>
  count(genre, month) |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = share, color = genre)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = 0.195, label = "Halloween:\n18% of horror releases",
           color = "#e11d48", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 0.14, label = "Comedy stays steady\nall year",
           color = "#f5c451", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 0.21)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = genre_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Studios release horror when audiences want to be scared",
    subtitle = "Share of each genre's movies released in each month",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: The Numbers, via TidyTuesday (807 comedies, 295 horror movies)"
  ) +
  theme_fear()
```

::: {.dropcap}
Comedies come out at about the same pace all year, with no month getting more than about 10% of them. Horror is different. Almost one in five horror movies in this data opened in October, more than twice the share of any month in winter. Studios know when audiences are in the mood for fear, and they plan around it.
:::

::: {.pullquote}
Almost one in five horror movies opens in October.
:::

That pattern fits what psychologists say about why people enjoy being scared. Halloween makes fear social and playful: haunted houses, costumes, and scary movies are things people do together, in a setting where they know they are safe. In that context a horror film is less a threat and more a shared thrill, and the relief at the end becomes part of the fun.

Comedy does not need a season, because the need it meets, relief from everyday stress, never goes away. Put side by side, the two genres show two different reasons people turn to movies: some feelings we seek out at certain times, and some we need all the time.
